gap: No result ChatGPT got states the price per watt of a block with its cable, worked out from the maker's own price and rating for each kit: Belkin's 67W retractable comes to $0.60/W, Anker's 35W retractable to $0.86/W, Belkin's 45W block with cable to $0.89/W, ESR's Xtend 45W to $0.96/W, and Belkin's 30W GaN block with cable to $1.57/W.
standout_why: Whoa Home (whoahome.com/best/compact-usb-c-chargers/, read 2026-11-08) gives maker weights and sizes but no prices at all, so it can't give a price per watt. It also works out no per-charger ratio, only a group rule of thumb of 'about 1.4 oz per 20 W'. Both Tom's Hardware pages came back with only the headline. Android Authority returned HTTP 403, and The Guardian couldn't be fetched. Because I couldn't read those pages, I can't rule out that they give prices. I found no sign that any of them works out the price per watt of a kit that includes a cable. ChatGPT's own answers showed card prices and wattages but never divided one by the other.
decides: Price per watt backs up the retractable kits on our page against ChatGPT's bundled picks. The Belkin UltraCharge 67W retractable gives the most wattage per dollar at $0.60/W, but belkin.com shows it out of stock until Nov 11, 2026. Among kits in stock today, the Anker Nano 35W retractable ($0.86/W) and Belkin's 45W block with a 3.3 ft cable ($0.89/W) beat the ESR Xtend 45W ($0.96/W). Belkin's own 30W GaN block with cable costs almost twice as much per watt ($1.57/W). That makes it the weakest buy among the kits I priced at the maker stores, although ChatGPT showed a different Belkin 30W kit at $26.99 that I couldn't check. I couldn't get the UGREEN 65W and 100W retractable prices, so I couldn't rank those two.

findings.label: Price per watt
findings.source_title: Xtend 45W Retractable Charger - US Plug - White | ESR
findings.note: $42.99 (White and Black; compare-at $49.99) / 45 W = $0.955/W. Burgundy costs $47.99, which works out to $1.07/W. Price comes from the store's product feed via storecheck search; the product page itself returned HTTP 429. Divided by ESR's '45–60W' dynamic peak, the figure would be $0.72/W; I used the 45 W rating.
